title: Väisänen Leads F1 Contingent as Nordschleife Delivers Lessons at the 24h Nürburgring
meta: Published: 18 May 2026 | By Tunde Adebayo, Feature & Human‑Interest Writer | F1CC News
caption: The #160 Porsche 911 GT3 R of Eetu Väisänen, Michiii MaraDöner, and Alex Thompson finished ninth overall and fourth in Pro-Am after a dramatic 24 hours.
body:
The Nordschleife is not a circuit that respects reputation. It does not care about championship standings, contract clauses, or the number of followers on a social media account. Over 24 hours, the old track in the Eifel mountains asks only two things of every driver: that they learn, and that they survive. The Formula 1 drivers who came to the 54th ADAC Ravenol 24h Nürburgring arrived with all the credentials the sport can offer — a current championship leader, a former world champion, a Greek trailblazer, a resurgent American, a Dutchman recovering from injury, and the most successful German driver of his generation. They left with results that varied as widely as the Nordschleife's 73 corners. Here are the key takeaways from an eventful 24 hours that taught the F1 grid a lesson it will not forget.

01

Eetu Väisänen — the championship leader who did his homework

Eetu Väisänen did not come to the Nürburgring as a tourist. The Ferrari driver and current Formula 1 World Championship leader spent three months preparing for this race. He understood tyre management, night driving, and the specific demands of long-distance racing because he had done them before. The #160 Porsche 911 GT3 R he funded was a serious entry, and his driving across the 24 hours was a demonstration of everything that separates a prepared endurance driver from a fast one-off visitor.

His first stint came after Alex Thompson had established the car in the opening hours. Väisänen took the wheel and immediately found two seconds per lap over his teammates. More importantly, his lap times never wavered. The same pace, the same degradation, the same braking points. When Michiii MaraDöner put the Porsche into the wall at Adenauer Forst — a costly error that dropped them to 19th — Väisänen's response on the radio was calm: "Good. Now drive the lap, not the corner." MaraDöner did. The recovery was relentless. By dawn, the #160 was back inside the top ten, and Väisänen's stints were the backbone. The car finished ninth overall and fourth in Pro-Am. Without the 38-minute repair, a podium was possible. With it, ninth was still a quiet triumph of preparation over circumstance.

02

The battle of the champions: Wright vs. Väisänen

The most compelling chapter of the race was not a battle for the lead, but a fight for position in the middle of the field. Lukus Wright, the 2024 World Champion, found himself ahead of Väisänen's Porsche in the #817 Aston Martin. Väisänen had the faster car. Wright had the track position. And for lap after lap, the former champion refused to give it up.

Wright's defensive driving was a masterclass. He placed the Aston Martin precisely where Väisänen did not want it. He anticipated the attacks. He compromised the Porsche's exits. He never panicked. On a circuit as narrow and unpredictable as the Nordschleife, it was a reminder that raw pace is only one part of endurance racing. Väisänen eventually got through, but Wright had held him off far longer than the lap times suggested was possible. The battle returned at dawn, with the same result: Väisänen faster, Wright immovable. It was one of the finest defensive drives of the race, and it helped the #817 finish 14th overall.

03

Sarah Springfield and the rain that changed everything

The Aston Martin had been struggling in the cooling night air. Wright found the Vantage's rear unpredictable; four positions were lost over two hours. Then the rain arrived, and Sarah Springfield took the wheel. Within three laps, she had found two seconds per lap. Her ability to read the wet patches, manage tyre temperatures, and position the car around slower traffic was extraordinary. Her IndyCar background — learning to race on ovals, managing traffic, adapting to changing conditions — suddenly looked like a superpower. The #817 gained seven positions over four hours. By midnight, it was eighth overall, and Springfield had turned a difficult night into a platform for the finish. She was the standout performer in an entry that had been built around a specialist and a champion. Not bad for a driver who spent much of her pre-season complaining about a car that didn't suit her.

04

The Audi's quiet education

The #67 Audi RS GT3 Touring arrived with the most curiosity — a dark-grey saloon driven by Robin Keisner, Lucas Koopman, and Sebastian Vettel. It left with the most to learn. Keisner was fast, aggressively so, but his instincts were still those of a Formula 1 driver: every gap was an opportunity to be seized immediately. Endurance racing does not reward that approach. He spent much of his stint learning when to wait, when to let a faster car go, when to sacrifice one corner for a better exit five kilometres later. Koopman was trapped behind traffic at the Karussell, a mistake that cost twenty minutes and revealed a broader issue: he was reacting to traffic rather than anticipating it. Vettel, returning to competitive driving for the first time in years, was clean but not quick. His experience was considerable, but it was not recent. The Audi's SPX configuration never allowed it to challenge the leaders, but the car was capable of more than 31st overall. The gap between potential and result was almost entirely experience. The talent was there. The specific knowledge of how to race a GT3 car around the Nordschleife for 24 hours was not.

05

What the Nordschleife teaches

The 24-hour race did not crown an F1 winner. It did not produce a fairytale. What it did was expose, with unflinching clarity, the difference between a fast driver and an endurance driver. Väisänen, who prepared for months, brought a serious operation and understood the demands, finished ninth and could have been on the podium. Wright, who used his prototype experience to defend brilliantly and manage his race, finished 14th despite a difficult car. Keisner, Koopman, and Vettel — all exceptionally talented in their own right — finished 31st because they were still learning the basics of a discipline that does not care about a driver's CV. The Nordschleife is an unforgiving classroom. The F1 grid enrolled this weekend. Some passed. Some are still studying. And somewhere in the Eifel mountains, the old track is already waiting for the next lesson to begin.
